title: How Engineers Think About Systems
subtitle: It's not just code, it's the decisions behind what happens when you press enter.
intro: You type google.com and press enter. In one second, your key press travels from a keyboard chip to a data center and back.
takeaway: Great engineering is tracing what happens step by step, from key press to server response.

sections.heading: Analogy: sending a letter across a city
sections.body:
Think of your browser request like mailing a letter.

You write the address (google.com), hand it to a local post office (your router), it travels through sorting hubs (the internet), reaches the destination building (Google's server), and a reply comes back along the same chain.

Every stop has a job, and if one stop is confused, the letter is lost. That chain is what engineers study next.

sections.heading: Why does this exist? To see the hidden steps
sections.body:
The repo github.com/alex/what-happens-when exists to answer one interview question in full detail: what happens when you type google.com and press enter?

A distributed system is many computers working together like one. A browser is your app for viewing the web. Networking is the rules they use to talk.

The repo lists every tiny step: the 'g' key press, an interrupt line, a KeyPress event, parsing the URL, and checking if it's a search term.

Seeing all steps helps you debug faster, but what if one step breaks?

sections.heading: What can go wrong? One missing detail breaks the flow
sections.body:
Real systems fail in small places you skipped.

- The URL parse fails and you search instead of navigating
- The network drops before the server answers
- The server reply is slow, so the browser waits

Production architecture is how companies design for these failures. Test automation is programs that check failures for you.

Learn the full path first, then you can predict where it will break.

steps.narration: You press 'g' and the keyboard sends an interrupt signal.
Browser receives KeyPress event and parses google.com as URL.
Request travels through your router and internet hubs.
Google's server receives request and prepares response.
Response travels back and browser renders the page.

quiz.q: Why does the 'what-happens-when' repo list every tiny step from key press to server?
options: To understand decisions and flow across systems
To avoid using the command line
quiz.why: The repo teaches engineering reasoning, not just code, by tracing the full browser-to-server chain.

quiz.q: What fails first if usage grows 100x and you never traced the network steps?
options: Network or server bottlenecks cause slow or dropped requests
quiz.why: Without understanding networking and distributed systems, traffic overloads routers and servers first.

quiz.q: What is a distributed system in plain words?
options: Many computers working together like one system
quiz.why: It's many machines coordinating over a network to act as a single service.
